items.description: Another Small Victory For Mortgage Rates By: Matthew Graham 1 Hour, 13 Min ago The present week continues to be rather uneventful for mortgage rates , although not at all unpleasant. It began with Monday largely holding in line with Friday's latest levels. While those were the highest in several weeks, we've made slow and steady progress since then. Each of the past 3 days has resulted in modest improvement with today's installment being the smallest so far at only 0.01%. The only caveat is that rates have needed some help in order to keep this gentle progress intact. A vast majority of "help" since early-to-mid October has come in the form of a stock market correction and general concerns over the sustainability of the AI boom. This has resulted in bond yields frequently correlating with major stock market averages like the NASDAQ or S&P. Today was no exception. Bonds were slightly weaker at first (thus implying slightly higher mortgage rates). It wasn't until stocks began to swoon around 10am ET that bond yields dropped, thus allowing mortgage lenders to set today's rates a bit lower than they otherwise could have. items.title: Anthropic's Record IPO Reverberates Across Data Center Sector
items.description: Anthropic raised $81.3B in the largest-ever stock market debut Thursday, briefly driving the Claude maker’s valuation north of $2T and delivering a vote of confidence for an artificial intelligence infrastructure boom that has faced growing scrutiny from investors. Wikimedia Commons/TechCrunch Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in 2023 Shares began trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market at $111.50 and climbed as high as $114.99 midday Thursday before dipping back below $100 — but still well above the company’s $83 offering price and the $70-to-$78 range Anthropic had anticipated earlier this month. The debut surpasses the previous initial public offering record set by rival AI firm SpaceX in June. The offering comes at a turbulent moment for the AI trade and the data center and digital infrastructure sector supporting it. Investors have grown increasingly uneasy about the staggering sums tech giants are spending to fund an infrastructure construction boom that has yet to generate commensurate returns. Rising community opposition and political headwinds in the wake of this month’s midterm elections have added another layer of uncertainty. The anxiety has been felt in public markets, with several companies tied closely to the AI data center boom delaying planned IPOs in recent weeks amid concerns about valuations and investor appetite for AI. Anthropic's debut may provide a counterpoint to that narrative and a direct boost to the data center sector. The IPO gives one of the world’s largest AI labs a massive pool of capital, a significant portion of which will flow toward computing capacity and data centers. Bryn Talkington, managing partner of Requisite Capital Management, told CNBC on Thursday that Anthropic becoming a public company also provides transparency into a major demand driver for digital infrastructure that has previously been lacking. This could give investors confidence that tech’s AI infrastructure spending spree will deliver returns. “This raise solidifies the capex spend,” Talkington said. “Now you have a real player that’s not being marked up by VC companies. You have a real player — SEC, quarterly earnings — and that creates transparency and accountability, which I think is a wonderful thing.” Anthropic’s move to the public markets coincides with a strategic shift that is expected to make the firm a major player in the data center landscape. In its S-1 prospectus filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission in October, Anthropic disclosed plans to reduce its reliance on cloud providers by leasing dedicated data centers at significant scale and operating its own computing hardware inside them. The strategy marks a departure for a company that has previously relied almost entirely on cloud providers like Amazon , Google and Microsoft for its computing power. Through the initiative, Anthropic Direct, leased data centers under Anthropic’s control will account for a growing share of the $542B to $567B the company plans to spend on computing infrastructure in the coming years, it said in the S-1 filing. Anthropic doesn't intend to develop data centers itself. Third-party providers will secure land and power, build facilities to Anthropic’s specifications and operate them on its behalf. The initiative is already moving beyond the planning stage, with Anthropic entering into purchase and lease agreements for Anthropic Direct, according to its SEC filing. “As our compute requirements have scaled, we have transitioned to a hybrid model in which, in addition to purchasing compute as a cloud service, we also procure specialized AI accelerators directly and operate this hardware in dedicated data center facilities leased and operated on our behalf, to our specification,” the company wrote in its SEC filing. But the company also said in its SEC filing that challenges building data centers will present a risk for the company, and the headwinds facing data center development have only increased since. November’s midterms saw voters across the U.S. approve local moratoriums and other measures to restrict data center development, while elections in key markets like Texas and Georgia produced new governors and other state officials who campaigned on limiting data centers. Democratic control of both chambers of Congress is also expected to bring greater scrutiny for the industry. Speaking with CNBC on Thursday morning, Anthropic President Daniela Amodei said the company will prioritize local input in its data center build-out to ensure communities don’t feel that the technology “is happening to them.” She also said the company is committed to paying for any increases in the cost of grid power that may occur due to the firm’s data centers. “From our perspective, building data centers is something where we also need to listen to what it is that those communities want and help to bring forward that future as well,” she said, adding that the company is aiming to “make sure that any cost increase is not borne by the consumer.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Anthropic , Artificial Intelligence , Claude , Dario Amodei , NASDAQ

items.title: U.S. Retail Monthly Foot Traffic & Sales Analysis | October 2026
items.description: U.S. Retail Monthly Foot Traffic & Sales Analysis | October 2026 Nov 19, 2026 Colliers Retail Market Intelligence October retail spending surges as early holiday shopping fuels sales and traffic growth. Download Report Experts Nicole Larson Senior Manager, National Retail Research | U.S. Anjee Solanki National Director, Retail Services & Practice Groups Summary Analysis U.S. retail sales maintained strong momentum in October, rising 6.9% year over year while foot traffic increased 1.6%. Core retail sales grew 5.5%, with underlying volumes increasing 2.8%, signaling stronger consumer demand as the holiday shopping quarter began. Gas station sales surged 30.1%, contributing to overall sales growth, while early holiday promotions helped lift non-store sales by 10.1%. Apparel continued to attract shoppers seeking value and seasonal purchases. Apparel sales increased 4.9%, with underlying volumes rising 1.2% as consumers favored discounted mid- and premium-priced merchandise. Clothing foot traffic climbed 6.4%, while department store visits jumped 11.3%, highlighting strong in-store engagement ahead of the holidays. Electronics spending remained strong, with sales increasing 7.6% despite a 3.4% decline in store visits. Product innovation and replacement demand helped support spending, even as consumers became more selective about where and how they shop. Furniture and furnishings sales rose 2.2%, with foot traffic increasing 2.1%, suggesting gradual improvement in home-related spending despite ongoing housing market challenges. Experiences and hobbies continued to draw consumers. Theater and music venue visits surged 28.5%, attractions increased 11.4%, and hobbies, gifts and crafts traffic climbed 17.9%. Meanwhile, grocery sales grew just 1.2%, with underlying volumes declining 0.5%, reflecting continued pressure on household budgets and a shift toward value-oriented shopping channels. Top-performing brands include Five Below, Ross Dress for Less, Barnes & Noble, Ollie's Bargain Outlet, BJ's Wholesale Club, Nordstrom Rack, Dollar Tree, Grocery Outlet, Carter's & OshKosh B'gosh, and Total Wine & More. items.title: Houston new-home sales dip to lowest level of 2026
items.description: Houston new-home sales dip to lowest level of 2026 by Emily Marek November 19, 2026 The state of new-home sales in Houston, featuring data from HomesUSA.com. Houston new-home sales declined marginally month over month in October, dipping to the lowest volume of the year so far, according to the Texas New Home Sales Report from HomesUSA.com . Buyers purchased 1,724 new homes during the month, down just slightly from September but down 12.7% from October 2025, when 1,975 new homes sold. Pending sales also declined both monthly and annually. Buyers contracted on 1,447 new homes in October, down 6.2% from 1,542 in September and 17.8% from 1,761 a year prior. Prices decreased monthly as well: The average was $402,169, down 1% from September but up 0.2% from October 2025. “Houston pending sales, a predictor of future sales, peaked five months ago in May and are now at their lowest levels since 2022,” said Ben Caballero , CEO of HomesUSA.com. “New-home sales are also at their lowest levels since 2022. New-home prices are following a similar downward trend.” Meanwhile, days on market increased nine days year over year, but remained essentially flat month over month at 98 days. “Don’t misunderstand what Houston’s days on market is telling us year over year. items.title: Office Development Hits 10-Year Low as Demand for Top Space Climbs
items.description: National CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. National + Weekender | November 19, 2026 By: Amy Wolff Sorter Office Development Hits 10-Year Low as Demand for Top Space Climbs Sandy Romero, Cushman & Wakefield Not so long ago, there was too much office supply and not enough vacancy. Then, there’s now. Cushman & Wakefield’s Global Office Supply report said that global office development is at its lowest level in a decade. With 580 million square feet under construction during Q3 2026, “the under-construction pipeline is 45% below its Q3 2017 peak of 1.04 billion square feet,” the report said. Meanwhile, in the United States, space under construction is at 23 million square feet, down 83% from its 2020 high. At the same time, “occupiers keep gravitating to high-quality, amenitized buildings, and that space is being absorbed faster than it can be replaced. That is pushing Class A vacancy down and supporting rent growth,” Sandy Romero, head of office & alternatives, global research at Cushman & Wakefield , told Connect CRE. It’s All About the Money Quite simply, the slowdown in construction and deliveries is because “building costs have risen faster than consumer prices,” the report explained. Supply chain disruptions, energy and shipping cost shocks, and labor shortages are among the reasons. Additionally, U.S. base rates stood at 3.75% in the third quarter, with further increases expected into early 2027. To assess whether new projects make financial sense, Cushman & Wakefield relied on economic rent, the minimum rent a new office building must earn to be profitable. Economic rent combines land acquisition costs, construction, operational expenses, leasing, developer margins and borrowing costs incurred during the development. On average, North American market rents were about 6% below economic rents. But those rents vary by city. New York, NY: Market rents of $156.64 per square foot are nearly 60% above economic rent of $98.69. About 6.4 million square feet were under construction as of the third quarter, nearly double the level of a year earlier. More than 2.5 million square feet is also under renovation as owners respond to tenants’ push for better space. Miami, FL: Class A starting rents are up 39% over three years, and Class A vacancy is 16%, down 180 basis points from a year ago. The pipeline of 1.8 million square feet is nearly three times last year’s level. “Among the metros, Miami is already there,” Romero said. Dallas, TX: Romero said that class A vacancy fell nearly 230 basis points (bps) over the past year to 26.3%, while starting rents are up 36% over three years. She expects build-to-suit and renovation projects to lead in the near term. “If vacancy keeps tightening, speculative projects could start to be planned in the next couple of years,” she added. Boston, MA: Market rents averaged $78.59 per square foot in 2026, 8% below economic rent of $85.38. No projects are under construction or renovation. Market rents are projected to rise above economic rent in 2029, driven by strong demand for newer Class A space. San Francisco, CA: Market rents of $98.43 per square foot are just 4% below economic rent of $102.94, the narrowest gap among markets still below the break-even point. Class A vacancy remains high at 31.1%, while the pipeline has been empty for almost four years. Chicago, IL: Chicago has the widest gap. Market rents of $84.56 per square foot are 10% below, meaning new construction isn’t likely to make financial sense until 2032. Los Angeles, CA: Romero said Los Angeles is furthest from the break-even point. Class A vacancy averaged 25.8% in the third quarter. “Class A starting rents are up 16% over three years, but that hasn’t kept pace with construction costs and other pressures,” Romero observed. Another potential quandary is federal fund rate hikes. However, Romero pointed out that such increases count but aren’t a deciding factor in development. “The economic rent needed to justify a project does include the cost of capital, and an additional hike could push out viability timelines modestly,” she explained. “But rent growth is the bigger lever, since demand for top-tier space is already lifting rents.” Class B and—Oversupply? The word “oversupply” can send jitters throughout the commercial real estate sector. It’s also an interesting term for office construction. Romero said that despite issues such as the doubling of construction in places like New York City, overbuilding won’t be an issue in the current cycle. “New York’s inventory shrunk by 1.6% over the past three years,” she explained. “Annual completions have averaged 1.8 million square feet, about 45% below the 10-year average of 3.2 million.” Additionally, rents and demand are high enough to support new development. There is also plenty of Class B space, but that’s not a cure-all for demand. Romero said that value-seeking tenants could take on the older, less fancy space. “However, tenants looking for highly amenitized space for their workforce won’t see Class B as a substitute,” she commented. Owners wishing to compete would need to upgrade to Class A standards, where the building allows. “Where it doesn’t, they may face prolonged vacancy or benefit from conversion to another use,” Romero said. items.title: Home Purchase Loans Fall to Lowest Third-Quarter Level Since 2012
items.description: Home Purchase Loans Fall to Lowest Third-Quarter Level Since 2012 by ATTOM Team | Nov 19, 2026 | Mortgage Origination , Real Estate News - Recent Articles Home purchase lending falls 9 percent quarter-over-quarter to 729,968 loans; Refinance lending drops 16 percent quarter-over-quarter to 561,290 loans IRVINE, Calif. – Nov. 19, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, today released its U.S. Residential Property Mortgage Origination Report for the third quarter of 2026, showing purchase and refinance lending slowed from the previous quarter as mortgage rates climbed and home purchase loans fell to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012. A total of 1.29 million purchase and refinance mortgages secured by residential property (1 to 4 units) were originated in the third quarter, down 12 percent from the previous quarter and 15 percent from a year earlier. Total loan volume reached $498.1 billion, down 15 percent quarterly and 12 percent year-over-year. The quarterly slowdown was driven by declines in both home purchase and refinance lending. Purchase loans fell 9 percent from the previous quarter to 729,968, marking the lowest third-quarter total since 2012. Purchase loans were down 12 percent from a year earlier, even as the average purchase loan amount rose 3 percent over the same period to $411,756. “The increase in refinance activity we saw late last year and into early this year cooled in the third quarter, with refinancing declining more than purchase lending,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “Purchase loans also slipped to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012, as higher mortgage rates and elevated average purchase loan amounts continued to strain affordability for many buyers.” Purchase lending slips quarterly in most markets Purchase lending totaled $300.6 billion in the third quarter, down 10 percent from the previous quarter and 10 percent below year-ago levels. Purchase loans accounted for 56.5 percent of all purchase and refinance originations, up from 54.5 percent in both the second quarter of 2026 and the third quarter of 2025. Purchase activity declined quarterly in 73.6 percent of analyzed metro areas with a population of 200,000 or more and sufficient data. Among metros with populations above 1 million, the largest quarterly increases were in Buffalo, NY (up 61 percent); Memphis, TN (up 50 percent); Rochester, NY (up 32 percent); New York, NY (up 22 percent); and Hartford, CT (up 20 percent). The steepest quarterly drops among large metros were in Salt Lake City, UT; New Orleans, LA; Denver, CO; Atlanta, GA; and Richmond, VA. Refinancing activity falls sharply quarter-over-quarter Refinancing activity fell 16 percent quarter-over-quarter to 561,290 loans, the lowest quarterly total since the second quarter of 2024, and was 19 percent below the third quarter of 2025. Refinance originations accounted for 43.5 percent of all purchase and refinance loans, down from 45.5 percent in both the previous quarter and a year earlier. Refinance lending declined quarterly in 89.4 percent of analyzed metro areas, with the steepest quarterly drops among large metros in San Jose, CA; Dallas, TX; San Francisco, CA; Austin, TX; and Louisville, KY. FHA and VA loan shares decline quarterly Loans backed by the Federal Housing Administration accounted for 15.7 percent of all purchase and refinance originations in the third quarter, down from 16.1 percent in the second quarter and 17.9 percent a year earlier. VA-backed loans represented 6.9 percent of originations, down from 8.2 percent in the second quarter and 7.2 percent a year earlier, the lowest share since the second quarter of 2024. Mortgage rates climb above 7 percent by early October Mortgage rates trended higher during the quarter. According to Freddie Mac, the average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage rose from 6.43 percent in early July to 7.28 percent by early October, adding pressure to an already constrained housing market. Home purchase lending dropped 9 percent quarter-over-quarter to 729,968 loans, the lowest third-quarter level since 2012, while refinance lending fell 16 percent quarter-over-quarter to 561,290 loans. Report methodology ATTOM analyzed recorded mortgage and deed of trust data for single-family homes, condos, town homes and multi-family properties of two to four units for this report. This report covers purchase and refinance loan originations. Each recorded mortgage or deed of trust was counted as a separate loan origination. Dollar volume was calculated by multiplying the total number of loan originations by the average loan amount for those loan originations. items.title: Brookfield Bets $110M On Resorts Company Rolling Up Independent Campgrounds
items.description: Unsplash/Andre Ouellet Brookfield Asset Management plans to spend $110M to buy a minority stake in a company that is buying up independent campgrounds with the expectation that the pandemic-era recreation boom is more than a fleeting trend. BAM is getting into business with Open Road Resorts, which has campgrounds across the country, including near Yellowstone National Park and in New York’s Finger Lakes region, Bloomberg reported . Open Road will use the money to acquire more campgrounds. The properties usually have RV sites as well as glamping tents and full-season sites for campers looking to post up for extended stays. Luxury RV campgrounds made up roughly 20% of the outdoor hospitality industry last year. The business was valued then at between $8B and $9B but received such heavy investment that it was expected to grow up to $30B in the next five years, Bisnow previously reported . Open Road was founded in 2019. In 2024, it raised capital from firms including consumer product investor L Catterton and recreational vehicle-maker Thor Industries Inc. to acquire RV parks, upgrade facilities and improve booking and revenue management systems. The changing demographics of RV owners, now skewing younger and wealthier, have fueled the push for upgrades and added amenities at RV parks. Brookfield and other institutional investors have placed money in more nontraditional real estate assets as the market has changed since the pandemic. Aside from campgrounds, firms are buying marinas and have plowed billions into industrial outdoor storage . NYC Capital Markets: Volume Moderates but Remains on Track for Recovery Year After four quarters of sustained recovery, investment sales slowed in the third quarter. Dollar volume totaled $5.6 billion, a 30.7% quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) decline and the first quarter since Q2 2025 to fall short of at least $8.0 billion. Investor confidence, which had steadily improved over the last year, was tempered by rising interest rates, uncertainty around the broader economy and geopolitical conditions, and the historically consistent trend of an election cycle pause. Despite the slowdown, the year-to-date (YTD) dollar volume total of $22.0 billion remains virtually unchanged from the same period last year, while the year’s annualized pace of $29.3 billion would represent a 23.3% increase over the 2020 cyclical low. In Q3 2026, there were 517 transactions involving the sale of 578 properties—an 18.2% year-over-year (YOY) decrease in properties sold. Average pricing for core property types across New York City fell to $504 per square foot (psf), a 0.6% decrease from the 2025 average. Cap rates for core property types have continued to inch higher in 2026 and now stand at an average of 7.13%. Sector Highlights Office: Dollar volume in Q3 2026 dipped to $1.4 billion, bringing the YTD total to $5.5 billion, only 7.8% below the same period last year. Although activity remains muted compared to historical levels, the investor pool is steadily expanding, with deals this quarter completed by a diverse mix of institutional, REIT, private capital, and user-purchasers. The average deal size declined for the third consecutive quarter, to $46.8 million, as smaller private capital players deployed more capital into value-add strategies for discounted and underutilized assets. At the same time, larger investors remain attracted to well-positioned, sizeable Class A assets with favorable tenancy and capital improvement conditions. Pricing has declined nominally this year, down 4.2% to $478 psf. Multifamily: Although combined dollar volume for elevator and walk-up properties slowed to $1.1 billion in Q3 2026, the YTD total of $4.8 billion falls only 11.7% short of the total from the same period last year, which marked the strongest year since 2022. Similar to the office sector, multifamily demand is starkly bifurcated between market-rate, newly-constructed, often luxury assets versus majority-rent-regulated, deeply discounted offerings—though both segments are exhibiting encouraging momentum. Substantial renter demand has kept vacancy at historic lows and attracted a growing pool of capital from both core/core-plus investors as well as value-add players. Development: Volume pulled back slightly to $831.6 million in Q3 2026, but the sector remains on pace to finish at $5.0 billion: if achieved, 2026 and 2025 would be the only two years since 2019 to surpass that benchmark. Depressed land values and a still-limited supply pipeline continued to drive activity. That momentum, previously focused in Manhattan, has begun to spread to the city’s secondary markets: four out of the five largest development transactions this quarter were located in the Outer Boroughs, totaling $249.6 million across 1.3 million buildable square feet. Increased demand has continued to support pricing recovery, with the citywide price per buildable square foot rising 6.4% YOY to $227, the highest average since 2019. Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . items.description: Monthly Housing Payments Fell to Lowest Level in Nearly 2 Months–But Rates Are Climbing Again Published on November 19th, 2026 by Dana Anderson Home prices are slipping and house hunters have more room to negotiate. But mortgage rates that are going back up could make the math harder for would-be buyers. What to know about the U.S. housing market for the four weeks ending November 15: Home-sale prices edged down for the fourth week in a row. The median home-sale price was $388,516, down 0.4% year over year. That extends a streak that followed three years of increases. Monthly housing payments dropped to their lowest level in nearly 2 months. The median monthly mortgage payment was $2,723 at a 7.11% mortgage rate, the weekly average. This data is seasonally adjusted. Payments are down from $2,760 a week earlier but still up 8.2% from a year ago. The relief may not last: the daily average mortgage rate rose to the 7.5% range this week. Homebuying activity slipped to a new low. Pending home sales fell 0.3% from a week earlier to their lowest level in records dating back to 2021. They declined year over year in every metro we analyzed, with the steepest drops in Seattle (-30.4%), Denver (-26.1%) and San Diego (-24.7%). There are over half a million more home sellers than buyers throughout the U.S., and just 3 major metros are seller’s markets. items.title: Large Median Price Gap Keeps New Homes More Affordable Than Existing Homes
items.description: Large Median Price Gap Keeps New Homes More Affordable Than Existing Homes November 19, 2026 Rose Quint No Comments While housing remains largely unaffordable, a nearly $40,000 gap in the national median price of a new house vs. an existing home kept new construction more affordable relative to existing homes in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest data from the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)/Wells Fargo Cost of Housing Index (CHI). The CHI results from the third quarter of 2026 show that a family earning the nation’s median income of $106,800 needed 33% of its income to cover the mortgage payment on a median-priced new home (down from 34% in the second quarter). Low-income families, defined as those earning only 50% of median income, would have to spend 66% (down from 67%) of their earnings to pay for the same new home. The figures are higher for the purchase of existing homes in the U.S. A typical family would have to pay 36% of their income for a median-priced existing home while a low-income family would need to pay 73% of their earnings to make the same mortgage payment. The U.S. data for the percentage of earnings needed to purchase a new home in the third quarter is based on a national median new home price of $393,300, which is down 4.2% from $410,700 in the second quarter. Meanwhile, the corresponding price for an existing home was $432,900 in the third quarter, down 0.5% from $434,900 in the previous quarter. CHI is also available for 175 metropolitan areas, calculating the percentage of a family’s income needed to make the mortgage payment on an existing home based on the local median home price and median income in those markets. In eight out of 175 markets in the third quarter, the typical family is severely cost-burdened (must pay more than 50% of their income on a median-priced existing home). In 87 other markets, such families are cost-burdened (need to pay between 31% and 50%). There are 80 markets where the CHI is 30% of earnings or lower. The Top 5 Severely Cost-Burdened Markets San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, Calif., was the most severely cost-burdened market on the CHI, where 79% of a typical family’s income is needed to make a mortgage payment on an existing home. The five most severely cost-burdened markets were: San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, Calif. (79%) Urban Honolulu, Hawaii (73%) San Diego-Chula Vista-Carlsbad, Calif. (70%) San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont, Calif. (66%) Barnstable Town, Mass. (61%) Low-income families would have to pay between 122% and 157% of their income in all five of the above markets to cover a mortgage. The Top 5 Least Cost-Burdened Markets By contrast, Decatur, Ill., was the least cost-burdened market on the CHI, where typical families needed to spend just 17% of their income to pay for a mortgage on an existing home. The least cost-burdened markets were: Decatur, Ill. (17%) Elmira, N.Y. (18%) Peoria, Ill. (19%) Wichita Falls, Texas (20%) Springfield, Ill. (20%) Davenport-Moline-Rock Island, Iowa-Ill. (20%) Low-income families in these markets would have to pay between 34% and 41% of their income to cover the mortgage payment for a median-priced existing home. Visit nahb.org/chi for tables and details. items.title: Housing groups urge FHFA to delay condo reserve rule until 2028
items.description: Five housing and mortgage industry trade groups are asking the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) to delay a planned increase in condominium association reserve requirements by one year, citing implementation challenges and potential financing disruptions. In a Nov. 19 letter sent to FHFA Director Bill Pulte , the organizations asked the agency to direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to postpone the changes from Jan. 4, 2027, to Jan. 4, 2028. The new requirement would increase the minimum reserve allocation for applicable condominium project reviews from 10% to 15% of annual budgeted assessment income. The letter was signed by the Community Associations Institute , Community Association Roundtable , Community Home Lenders of America ( CHLA ), Housing Policy Council and National Association of Mortgage Brokers ( NAMB ). The groups said they support adequately funded condominium reserves but argued that associations, lenders and homeowners need more time to prepare for the change. Some have asked for change before. In June, NAMB asked the FHFA to delay upcoming Fannie and Freddie condo review and insurance standards by 12 months. But Fannie Mae retired its limited review process for condominium projects on Aug. 3. "Condominium project eligibility has already declined following recent changes to project review requirements, including the elimination of Limited Review options," the groups wrote. Outlining their concerns The coalition identified three primary concerns with the planned increase, stating that "the change could have unintended consequences for condominium financing and housing availability." First, many condominium associations operate on annual budget cycles and cannot easily adjust their funding midyear. Some may also need updated reserve studies, board approvals or homeowner consultations before changing their funding practices. The groups also said questions remain about how the new requirement will apply to existing budgets, recently completed reserve studies, major capital improvement projects and alternative funding arrangements. Lenders, servicers and condo management companies will also need time to update their systems, underwriting procedures and project reviews. Second, the groups warned that associations unable to meet the higher reserve requirement or qualify under an alternative reserve study provision could lose eligibility for conventional financing through the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs). The groups raised concerns that this could reduce the pool of potential buyers, make it more difficult for existing homeowners to sell or refinance, and put pressure on condo resale values. The impact could be particularly pronounced in older buildings, smaller communities and associations with more "modest-income" homeowners, the letter stated. Projects that lose conventional financing eligibility could become more reliant on nonagency or portfolio loans, which may be more expensive or less readily available. Lastly, the coalition said higher reserve contributions could add to housing costs at a time when homeowners are already facing elevated mortgage payments, property taxes , insurance premiums, maintenance expenses and association fees. Fannie Mae has estimated that the higher reserve requirement could add an average of $13 to $14 per month to condominium owners' costs, but the actual increase would vary by association, according to the coalition. Its accompanying analysis illustrated how the additional five percentage points could affect homeowners if the entire increase were funded through regular assessments. As part of the proposed one-year extension, the coalition urged FHFA to convene industry stakeholders to evaluate the financial and operational effects of the change, clarify how existing reserve studies and funding arrangements will be treated, and develop transition provisions for associations working toward adequate reserve funding. "We believe that strengthening condominium financial health and maintaining housing affordability should be complementary objectives," the letter said. items.title: Parkland Communities secures $50M development financing, begins Highland Brook in Dacula
items.description: Parkland Communities secures $50M development financing, begins Highland Brook in Dacula by John Yellig November 18, 2026 The financing was seeded with a $15 million loan to fund Highland Brook. Via Parkland Communities. Parkland Communities recently secured a $50 million borrowing-base production facility with Anchor Loans to grow its homebuilding operations, starting with its 103-home Highland Brook community in Dacula. The financing is solely dedicated to Parkland Communities' for-sale housing operations and was seeded with a $15 million loan to fund Highland Brook. The facility provides capital for developed lots, entitled land and development costs, as well as new home construction. Parkland said it will pursue residential land and developed lots across Georgia. "Periods of uncertainty create some of the best opportunities for companies that are prepared to act," Parkland President Jim Jacobi said. "While others may be pulling back, we're focused on growth. Our relationship with Anchor Loans gives us the ability to be selective, act fast and pursue the right land opportunities to bring new communities to market. We believe there is real value in being positioned to move when others are waiting. Parkland is buying." Parkland has communities at various stages of development across Georgia, including Parkside at Grove Landing in Warner Robins and Alder Creek in Cumming, which are now selling, as well as Brookwood Green in Snellville and Stonehaven Park in Stone Mountain, which broke ground this year. “We're pleased to work with Parkland and support its investment in new housing communities across Georgia,” said JP Ackerman, chief revenue officer at Anchor Loans. “Our ability to provide tailored financing from land acquisition through vertical construction allows Parkland to move strategically and capitalize on opportunities as they emerge. items.title: Multifamily Permitting’s Share Rebounds as Single-Family Declines
items.description: Multifamily Permitting’s Share Rebounds as Single-Family Declines by Chuck Ehmann Posted November 18, 2026 in Multifamily Construction Permits The share of multifamily permitting to total residential construction has varied greatly over the past sixty-plus years due to either stronger than normal multifamily permitting or weaker single-family construction. From 2000 through 2005, multifamily accounted for only about 18% to 21% of total permits. That was well below the multifamily booms of the 1970s and 1980s, when its share peaked near 47% in 1972 and returned to roughly 37% in 1985. During the 1990s, multifamily permitting averaged about 21% of total housing permits. The early-2000s housing bubble elevated permitting for both segments, but single-family grew faster. That held the multifamily share to about 18% in 2004 before the bust cut permitting for both, with its share bottoming at 14.6% in July 2009. Multifamily recovered faster, and the share has generally exceeded 30% since 2011 as renting as a lifestyle and other societal and economic factors boosted apartment demand. Unusual permitting spikes are evident in the chart ahead of New York’s tax-exempt program changes that pushed the ratio to 45.8% in June 2008 and 46.3% in June 2015. The February 2023 spike of 47.4%, the highest since 1973, came mainly from a slowdown in single-family development as interest and mortgage rates rose, coupled with a post-pandemic surge in multifamily. Single-family permitting recovered somewhat in 2024 and 2025 but has fallen off again recently, pushing the current ratio to 36.7% in October 2026. Seasonally adjusted multifamily permitting was at an annualized rate of 475,000 units in October, down 5.2% for the month and almost unchanged (-0.4%) from last October. Meanwhile, annualized single-family permitting of 772,000 units was down 8.7% from September’s rate and 12.9% from last year. That is the lowest annual rate for single-family since January 2023. The more volatile multifamily starts rate surged 25.5% from September’s revised annual figure to 433,000 units, a 22% increase from last year. September’s reported annual rate was the second lowest in 17 months. Single-family starts increased 4% from last month to 864,000 units but that was 3.2% lower than one year ago. However, both were down close to 10% for the year. The tally of multifamily units under construction was unchanged from September at 674,000 units and that rate was 3.2% lower than last October. items.title: Office REIT Sells Reston Property To Local Firm For 30% Of 2014 Price
items.description: Office Properties Income Trust, which emerged from bankruptcy in June, has offloaded a Reston, Virginia, office building for less than a third of its sale price 12 years ago. Google Maps The 135K SF office property at 1775 Wiehle Ave. in Reston, Virginia The REIT, managed by Massachusetts-based The RMR Group, sold the 135K SF property at 1775 Wiehle Ave. — which is just over half vacant — to Bethesda-based Polinger Co. for $12.1M. The sale closed Oct. 22, according to Fairfax County property records. That price is well below what it sold for in 2014, when First Potomac Realty Trust paid $41M for the asset. OPI gained control of the property three years later, when it acquired First Potomac. Polinger likes the supply-and-demand dynamics of the Reston office market, with growing appetite from defense and technology companies and a tightening supply as office parks are converted to residential, John Gordon, president of the firm's development arm, told Bisnow . "We think over the years that the value goes up tremendously because of the lack of new buildings and taking down the buildings and just this great location," he said. OPI did not respond to a request for comment, and a spokesperson for RMR declined to comment on its behalf. OPI is selling off large swaths of its now 16M SF office portfolio. The REIT, like many other office-heavy owners, was hit hard by post-pandemic tidal shifts in office capital markets. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October 2025, a year after notifying investors about doubts that it could continue operating in light of its maturing debt. During the restructuring process, OPI shed $714M in debt, leaving it with $1.7B in money owed. At the end of its restructuring, it said it had 31 properties totaling 3M SF on the market that it would sell to repay debts. As of the end of September, the REIT was under agreements to sell 15 office assets totaling more than 1.7M SF, according to its third-quarter report , including one more in Reston and two in Washington, D.C. OPI already sold 13 properties, totaling 1.5M SF, during the third quarter. Those were sold for a total of $143M, and OPI recorded a $5.5M loss on the sales. One of those sales was a 140K SF Dupont Circle office building, which it offloaded for $6.2M in September. On the 1775 Wiehle sale, OPI recorded a $2.3M loss on impairment of real estate. 1775 Wiehle, which was built in 2000, is just under 50% leased, Gordon told Bisnow . The building is anchored by law firm Odin Feldman Pittleman, which has a 35K SF long-term lease at the property, he said. Other tenants include law firm Goel & Anderson and Forge Financial Group. Polinger plans to put money into tenant improvement allowances and build out a full floor of spec suites, in addition to a spec-suite floor added by OPI. The company is seeing interest from medical tenants as well as engineering companies and government contracting firms, Gordon said. Polinger’s website says it manages 3M SF of office, retail and mixed-use space across the D.C. area, including office buildings in the District, Fairfax, Bethesda, Chevy Chase, Gaithersburg and Landover. This summer, the company offloaded a 235K SF Navy Yard office building to Matthew Jemal’s new investment firm, Jemal Equities. The $193.3M price for 99 M St. SE was 43% less than Polinger paid when it bought the property in 2019. For 1775 Wiehle, Newmark represented both sides of the transaction, Kassandra Saridakis, a capital markets managing director for the brokerage, told Bisnow. Jud Ryan, James Cassidy and Grant Marley represented the seller. Saridakis worked with Joe Donato, Andrew Asbill and Kevin Ridgway to arrange acquisition financing for Polinger. items.title: Why housing construction is sliding back toward COVID-era lows
items.description: The great housing construction boom that people have been cheering about for four years now looks to be on the cusp of falling to COVID-era lows. How is this possible when people have been saying for the past five years that we need to build more homes and Congress just passed the giant ROAD to Housing Act this summer — which was designed to help spur more construction. The old laws of economics still play out here; there simply isn’t enough housing demand to build more homes. This is something I wrote about back in June 2021 : when mortgage rates eventually rise this whole thing will reverse. Now, in November 2026, we are not that far away from the COVID-19 recession lows, as housing permits are already at COVID-19 recession levels and mortgage rates are above 7%. Building permits From Census : Building Permits: Privately-owned housing units authorized by building permits in October were at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1,295,000. This is 7.4 percent below the revised September rate of 1,398,000 and is 8.7 percent below the October 2025 rate of 1,418,000. Single-family authorizations in October were at a rate of 772,000; this is 8.7 percent below the revised September figure of 846,000. Authorizations of units in buildings with five units or more were at a rate of 475,000 in October. As we can see in the chart below, housing permits have been slowly falling for years and we are not only at levels last seen during the COVID-19 recession, but we’re on pace to hit the lows of that time period if this trend continues. And all this is happening when mortgage rates are close to 7.5% and the Fed is starting a new rate hike cycle. Single-family permits are not only close to the lows of 2022, but not that far from the COVID-19 recession lows either. Builders have done an admirable job keeping new home sales elevated enough to keep housing starts from falling further, but that has limits as profit margins fall. As you can see here, the single-family permits have taken a noticeable dive. Builders confidence at multiyear lows One question I got recently, which has merit: Why is builder confidence at multiyear lows, but new home sales have grown over the last few months? Just remember that the builder confidence index is tilted toward smaller homebuilders, not the big publicly traded homebuilders that are still buying down rates to move product. New home sales are still at 2019 levels, and so are housing starts and permits. If the big builders lose their ability to buy down rates, this sales data should eventually break below 2019 levels, but for now sales have operated within a small range for the past 10 years. Conclusion Since mortgage rates shot toward 7.60%, we have seen housing data turn very negative. Compare that to last year at this time, when mortgage rates were heading toward 6% and existing home sales hit a nine-month high. The big builders can only do so much to keep starts from falling more. For now, it doesn’t look good for housing construction in 2027, given where mortgage rates are at and the builders profit margins falling more and more. Related More:

items.title: Bank Branch Costs Hinge More on Market Than Management, JLL Finds
items.description: National CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. National + Weekender | November 19, 2026 By: Amy Wolff Sorter Bank Branch Costs Hinge More on Market Than Management, JLL Finds Erin Haglund, JLL In early 2026, a Wall Street Journal article said that bank branches were closing at a rapid rate, due to the continued rise of digital banking. Between 2019 and 2024, over 6,000 branches nationwide closed. However, U.S. banks opened more branches in the first half of 2026 than they closed, “reflecting the first sustained expansion since the financial crisis and a historic shift after more than a decade of post-crisis consolidation,” according to JLL’s just-released “The Cost of Running a Retail Bank Branch Network” report . “Digital banking has fundamentally changed how customers transact, but it hasn’t eliminated the need for personal interaction,” Erin Haglund, managing director, financial services at JLL , told Connect CRE. “In many ways, it has made the purpose of the physical branch more important and more specialized.” While this might be good news for customers who prefer their banking to be up close and personal rather than online, it can also mean higher operating costs for the banks in question. Location Determines Costs Many of the expenses boil down to a branch’s locale. “What stood out most was just how much of a branch’s operating cost is determined by the market itself, rather than the decisions a bank makes about managing its facilities,” Haglund said. The JLL report explained that across 12 U.S. markets, facilities operating cost per square foot is 2.6 times higher at the top than at the bottom. The expenses include repair and maintenance, cleaning, snow clearance and grounds maintenance, while excluding rent, pass-through charges from landlords and capital spending. Annual costs per square foot by market are: New York City: $24.35 Chicago: $15.18 New Jersey: $14.94 Long Island, NY: $14.83 Houston: $12.76 Dallas-Fort Worth: $12.24 Philadelphia: $12.12 Hartford, CT: $12.10 Seattle/Puget Sound: $11.40 Baltimore, MD: $10.50 Washington, DC metro: $10.36 Orange County, CA: $9.23 The gap results from wage levels, climate and building format versus portfolio management. “Banks have historically relied on national benchmarks, standardized contracts, and broad cost-reduction targets to drive efficiency,” Haglund said. “But our research reinforces that a lower-cost branch isn’t necessarily a better-managed branch, and a higher-cost branch isn’t necessarily inefficient.” Cost Negotiation: A Non-Starter The problem faced by branches and banks is that less than one-third of operating budgets can be divided into categories in which vendor negotiation can lead to lower prices. Here’s why: Landlords set service charges, which are the largest single line in the budget Maintenance costs are the result of vendor availability, rather than contracted rates For example, negotiating cleaning service costs doesn’t yield much in savings due to rising wages, benefit costs and turnover. The report said that interior cleaning costs 48% more in heavy-union markets than in right-to-work markets, while fire and life safety costs 83% more. Furthermore, a cleaning line that includes supplies, waste handling, pest control and exterior work averages $4.78 per square foot, compared with $3.19 for general interior cleaning alone. That’s roughly a 50% difference for the same physical work. Haglund said that focusing on structural market costs rather than operating costs can help. “That allows banks to focus resources where they can actually influence outcomes rather than chasing savings that may not be achievable,” she said. Another issue is the growing shortage of skilled trades professionals to maintain the physical branches. JLL research reported that approximately 2.1 million skilled trades positions could go unfilled by 2030. Banks compete for such workers with data centers, life sciences and advanced manufacturing, especially in Sun Belt metros where both are expanding. When equipment fails, and no technician is available, the cost goes beyond the repair bill. “From a financial perspective, labor shortages can increase emergency service premiums, extend repair timelines and drive higher costs for temporary solutions,” Haglund said. “Deferred maintenance can also accelerate equipment deterioration and create more significant capital expenditures down the road.” JLL recommended that banks secure technician capacity and response times before negotiating price. Haglund added that banks should pool maintenance demand across networks, so vendor partners could better plan staffing. Meanwhile, landlords should focus on coordinating building maintenance, replacing equipment before it wears out, and keeping an eye on building systems. “Ultimately, we need to shift from a reactive maintenance model to one that is more predictive, coordinated and focused on protecting operational continuity,” Haglund said. Then, There’s the Weather It’s no secret that climate change is impacting commercial real estate, including physical branches. Citing Climate Central, the JLL report said that billion-dollar weather disasters have struck the U.S. about every 16 days on average over the past decade, compared with every 82 days in the 1980s. A single regional event (think a hurricane or snowstorm) can impact every branch in a market at once. The bank that relies on a few vendors could find it needs them all at once. One solution is for bank branch budgets to incorporate expected weather-related variances. “The objective isn’t necessarily to avoid higher-risk markets; it’s to understand the exposure, evaluate the economics, and design the appropriate level of resilience into the network,” Haglund explained. executive_summary.text: 住宅建筑许可继续走弱：HousingWire 专栏作者认为，需求不足使建设接近疫情时期低位；Census 显示，10 月总许可年化为 1,295,000 套，较前一统计期修订值 1,398,000 下降 7.4%。其中，独栋住宅许可年化为 772,000 套，较前一统计期修订值 846,000 套下降 8.7%；五套及以上建筑许可年化为 475,000 套，住宅供给收缩与需求疲弱同时存在。文中还称按揭利率高于 7%，且美联储开始新一轮加息周期；对住宅资产持有者而言，后续应观察需求与融资条件变化对建设路径的影响。
executive_summary.text_en: Housing permits continued to weaken: a HousingWire columnist said insufficient demand is pushing construction toward COVID-era lows; Census reported October total permits at an annualized 1,295,000 units, down 7.4% from the prior revised period’s 1,398,000. Single-family permits were 772,000 annualized units, down 8.7% from the prior revised period’s 846,000; permits for buildings with five or more units were 475,000 annualized units, leaving supply contraction and weak demand in tension. The article also said mortgage rates were above 7% and the Fed was beginning a new hiking cycle; housing owners should watch how demand and financing conditions shape the construction pipeline.

outlook.text_en: Over the next 30 days, October Case-Shiller and FHFA house price indexes are scheduled for Nov. 24, followed on Nov. 25 by Census new residential sales and the NAR Pending Home Sales Index. Releases then include the BLS employment report on Dec. 4, the FOMC rate decision on Dec. 9, the NAHB Housing Market Index on Dec. 15, CPI and housing starts and building permits on Dec. 16, and existing-home sales on Dec. 17. MBA and Freddie Mac PMMS surveys are scheduled weekly on Wednesdays and Thursdays.
